source_text:
Isti igitur impuri spiritus, daemones , ut ostensum a magis, a philosophis et a Platone, sub statuis et imaginibus consecratis delitescunt et adflatu suo auctoritatem quasi praesentis numinis consequuntur, dum inspirant interim uates, dum fanis inmorantur, dum nonnumquam extorum fibras animant, auium uolatus gubernant, sortes regunt, oracula efficiunt, falsis pluribus inuoluta.
nam et falluntur et fallunt, ut et nescientes sinceram ueritatem et quam sciunt, in perditionem sui non confitentes. sic a caelo deorsum grauant et a Deo uero ad materias auocant, uitam turbant, somnos inquietant, inrepentes etiam corporibus occulte ut spiritus tenues morbos fingunt, terrent mentes, membra distorquent, ut ad cultum sui cogant, ut nidore altarium uel hostiis pecudum saginati, remissis quae constrinxerant, curasse uideantur.
hinc sunt et furentes, quos in publicum uidetis excurrere, uates et ipsi absque templo, sic insaniunt, sic bacchantur, sic rotantur: par et in illis instigatio daemonis, sed argumentum dispar furoris.
de ipsis etiam illa, quae paulo ante tibi dicta sunt, ut Iuppiter ludos repeteret ex somnio, ut cum equis Castores uiderentur, ut cingulum matronae nauicula sequeretur.
haec omnia sciunt pleraque pars uestrum ipsos daemonas de semetipsis confiteri, quotiens a nobis tormentis uerborum et orationis incendiis de corporibus exiguntur.
ipse Saturnus et Serapis et Iuppiter et quicquid daemonum colitis, uicti dolore quod sunt eloquuntur, nec utique in turpitudinem sui, nonnullis praesertim uestrum adsistentibus, mentiuntur.
ipsis testibus, esse eos daemonas, credite fassis: adiurati enim per Deum uerum et solum inuiti miseris corporibus inhorrescunt et uel exiliunt statim uel euanescunt gradatim, prout fides patientis adiuuat aut gratia curantis adspirat. sic Christianos de proximo fugitant, quos longe in coetibus per uos lacessebant.
ideo inserti mentibus imperitorum odium nostri serunt occulte per timorem: naturale est enim et odisse quem timeas, et quem metueris infestare, si possis. sic occupant animos et obstruunt pectora, ut ante nos incipiant homines odisse quam nosse, ne cognitos aut imitari possint aut damnare non possint.
thought_title: Demons hide in idols and deceive through false miracles
orientation: Octavius is continuing his reply to Caecilius, explaining how demons work through pagan idols, oracles, and possessions to deceive people and turn them from the true God.
pass_a_gloss: These impure spirits, demons, as shown by magi, by philosophers and by Plato, hide under statues and consecrated images and by their breath they obtain the authority as if of a present deity, while they inspire prophets in the meantime, while they linger in temples, while sometimes they animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flights of birds, rule lots, produce oracles, wrapped in many falsehoods. For they both are deceived and deceive, so that they both do not know the sincere truth and the truth which they know, they do not confess it, to their own destruction. Thus they weigh down from heaven to the earth and call away from the true God to material things, they disturb life, they trouble sleep, creeping also secretly into bodies as thin spirits they fashion diseases, they terrify minds, they distort limbs, so that they may force people to worship of themselves, so that, fattened by the smell of altars or by sacrifices of cattle, having released the things which they had bound, they may seem to have healed. Hence there are also the raging ones, whom you see running out into public, prophets themselves also without a temple, thus they rave, thus they revel like Bacchants, thus they whirl around: equal is in them the instigation of the demon, but the display of madness is different. From these same demons are also those things which were said to you a little before, that Jupiter demanded games again from a dream, that Castors were seen with horses, that a matron's girdle was followed by a little boat. All these things most part of you know that the demons themselves confess about themselves, as often as they are driven out from bodies by us with torments of words and fires of prayer. Saturn himself and Serapis and Jupiter and whatever demons you worship, overcome by pain they speak out what they are, and not at all to their own shame, especially when some of you are standing by, do they lie. By their own testimony, believe that they are demons, when they have confessed: for adjured by the true and only God, unwilling, they shudder in the miserable bodies and either leap out immediately or vanish gradually, as the faith of the sufferer helps or the grace of the healer breathes upon. Thus they flee Christians from nearby, whom they were provoking from afar in assemblies through you. Therefore inserted into the minds of the inexperienced they sow hatred of us secretly through fear: for it is natural both to hate whom you fear, and to attack whom you dread, if you can. Thus they occupy souls and block hearts, so that people begin to hate us before they know us, so that they cannot either imitate us once known or not condemn us.

choices.why: Keeps the adjective-noun order and the literal sense of 'impure' rather than the glossary's 'demons' for daemones, which appears separately in apposition.
Literal rendering of adflatu as breath or blowing, preserving the physical image of demonic influence.

choices.english: as if of a present deity
choices.why: Uses the glossary term 'deity' for numen and keeps the quasi conditional force.
rejected: as if of a present divine power
as if of a god present

choices.why: Literal rendering of inuoluta as wrapped, preserving the image of oracles being entangled in lies.

choices.english: they do not confess it, to their own destruction
choices.why: Keeps the reflexive sui as 'their own' and the purpose force of in perditionem.
rejected: to their own ruin they do not confess
not confessing it for their own destruction

choices.term: ut nidore altarium uel hostiis pecudum saginati
choices.english: so that, fattened by the smell of altars or by sacrifices of cattle
choices.why: Literal rendering of nidore as smell and saginati as fattened, preserving the grotesque image of demons feeding on sacrifices.
rejected: fed by the savor of altars
gorged on the odor of altars

pass_b_english: These impure spirits, then, are demons, as the magi, the philosophers, and Plato have shown. They hide beneath consecrated statues and images, and by their breath they gain the authority of a deity who seems to be present. Meanwhile they inspire prophets, linger in shrines, sometimes animate the fibers of entrails, guide the flight of birds, control lots, and produce oracles wrapped in many falsehoods.

For they are both deceived and deceive. They do not know the pure truth, and what truth they do know they do not confess, to their own destruction. So they weigh us down from heaven and call us away from the true God to material things. They disturb life, trouble sleep, and creeping secretly into bodies as fine spirits, they feign diseases, terrify minds, and twist limbs. They do this to force people to worship them, so that, fattened by the smell of altars or by sacrifices of cattle, they may seem to have cured what they themselves had bound.

From these same demons come also the madmen you see running through public places, prophets themselves even without a temple. That is how they rave, how they revel like Bacchants, how they whirl about. The demon's goading is the same in them, but the display of madness is different.

From these same demons come the stories I told you a little earlier: that Jupiter demanded games through a dream, that Castor and Pollux were seen with their horses, that a matron's girdle followed a little boat.

Most of you know that the demons themselves confess all this about themselves, whenever they are driven out of bodies by our torments of words and the fire of prayer. Saturn himself, and Serapis, and Jupiter, and whatever demons you worship, overcome by pain, speak out what they are. They do not lie to their own shame, especially when some of you are standing by.

Believe their own testimony, when they admit they are demons. For when they are adjured by the one true God, they shudder unwillingly in their wretched bodies, and either leap out at once or vanish gradually, as the faith of the sufferer helps or the grace of the healer breathes upon them. That is why they flee Christians at close range, though from a distance they attack them through you in your assemblies.

For this reason they creep into the minds of the ignorant and secretly sow hatred of us through fear. It is natural to hate someone you fear, and to attack someone you dread, if you can. So they seize souls and block hearts, so that people begin to hate us before they know us, lest, once they know us, they might either imitate us or be unable to condemn us.

problems.why: Latin says they feign (pretend) diseases, not actually create them.
problems.ruling: fingunt means 'feign/fake,' not 'create'; demons pretend diseases, not cause real ones—meaning changed.

fixed: Changed 'they create diseases' to 'they feign diseases': source 'morbos fingunt' means they pretend or feign diseases, not actually create them.

problems.quote: fattened by the smell of altars or by sacrifices of cattle
problems.why: Demons 'fattened' by smells is odd physically; refers to receiving nourishment from vapors.

edits.old: fattened by the smell of altars or by sacrifices of cattle
edits.new: nourished by the savor of altars or by sacrifices of cattle

fixed: The source 'nidore altarium uel hostiis pecudum saginati' means 'fattened by the smell of altars or by sacrifices of cattle'; 'fattened' is a literal rendering of 'saginati' and is not a mistranslation, but 'nourished by the savor of altars' is a more natural English rendering of the same idea, so I made the change.

last_rejected.why: Latin means 'drag down from heaven', not 'weigh us down from heaven'.
Latin 'auocant' means 'draw away, divert', not specifically 'call us away'.
last_rejected.fix: draw us away to material things

last_rejected.why: Latin means 'to the destruction of others' (sui = genitive plural of se), not 'their own destruction'.
last_rejected.ruling: in perditionem sui = into their own destruction

last_rejected.quote: They do not lie to their own shame
last_rejected.source_quote: nec utique in turpitudinem sui, nonnullis praesertim uestrum adsistentibus, mentiuntur
last_rejected.why: Latin means 'nor do they lie, certainly not to their own shame, especially with some of you standing by'—i.e., they tell the truth because they'd be ashamed to lie in front of witnesses. English inverts the sense.
last_rejected.fix: nor do they lie, certainly not to their own shame, especially with some of you standing by
last_rejected.ruling: nec ... mentiuntur = they do not lie to their own shame

last_rejected.quote: the grace of the healer breathes upon them
last_rejected.why: Latin 'adspirat' means 'blows upon, assists', but 'breathes upon them' suggests physical breath; 'assists' or 'blows' better captures the sense of divine help.
last_rejected.fix: the grace of the healer assists

last_rejected.why: Latin 'in coetibus per uos' means 'in assemblies through you' or 'through you in crowds'—the English order obscures that 'per uos' is the means, 'in coetibus' the place.
last_rejected.ruling: per uos = through you; placement okay

last_rejected.why: Latin 'inserti' means 'having crept in, insinuated', not 'creep into'—it's perfect passive participle indicating completed action.
last_rejected.ruling: inserti mentibus = having crept into minds; translation fits

last_rejected.quote: So they seize souls and block hearts
last_rejected.source_quote: sic occupant animos et obstruunt pectora
last_rejected.why: Latin says demons occupy minds (animus) and block hearts; English says they seize souls, changing the target from mind to soul.
last_rejected.fix: So they occupy minds and block hearts
last_rejected.ruling: animus commonly means 'soul' or 'mind' in Latin; 'seize' is within occupant's range. No meaning changed.

polish.changed: Clarified that the speaker is Octavius addressing Caecilius and other pagans, made pronoun references explicit, removed em dashes, smoothed sentence rhythm, and kept every claim and Scripture reference intact.

notes.quote: fattened by the smell of altars or by sacrifices of cattle
notes.why: Demons 'fattened' by smells is odd physically; refers to receiving nourishment from vapors.
